title: Arabic music
wiki_lead:
Arabic music (Arabic: الموسيقى العربية, romanized: al-mūsīqā l-ʿarabiyyah) is the music of the Arab world with all its diverse music styles and genres. Arabs have created varied styles of music with songs and instrumental ensembles in many linguistic varieties, with each country and region having their own folk, classical and modern musical styles.
Arabic music, which is based on the maqam system, has experienced a long history of exchange with other regional musical styles and genres. It represents the music of the people that make up the Arab world today.
wiki_excerpt:
Arabic music (Arabic: الموسيقى العربية, romanized: al-mūsīqā l-ʿarabiyyah) is the music of the Arab world with all its diverse music styles and genres. Arabs have created varied styles of music with songs and instrumental ensembles in many linguistic varieties, with each country and region having their own folk, classical and modern musical styles.
Arabic music, which is based on the maqam system, has experienced a long history of exchange with other regional musical styles and genres. It represents the music of the people that make up the Arab world today.


History


Pre-Islamic period
Pre-Islamic Arabia was the cradle of early achievements in music, musical theory and the development of musical instruments. In historical Yemen, the main center of pre-Islamic Arab sciences, literature and arts, musicians benefited from the patronage of the Kings of Sabaʾ who encouraged the development of music. For centuries, the Arabs of Hejaz recognized that the best Arabic music came from Yemen, and Hadhrami minstrels were considered to be superior musicians. 
Pre-Islamic Arabian peninsular music was similar to that of ancient Middle Eastern music.[citation needed] Most historians[who?] agree that there existed distinct forms of music in the Arabian peninsula in the pre-Islamic period between the 5th and 7th century AD. Arab poets of that time—called shu`ara' al-jahiliyah (Arabic: شعراء الجاهلية) or "Jahili poets", meaning "the poets of the period of ignorance"—used to recite poems sung with high notes.
Some people believed that Jinns revealed poems to poets and music to musicians. The choir at the time served as a pedagogic means where poets would recite their poems. Singing was entrusted to women with beautiful voices who would learn how to play some instruments used at that time such as frame drums, the lute or the rebab, and perform their songs while respecting the poetic metre. The compositions were simple and every singer would sing in a single maqam. Among the notable songs of the period were the huda (from which the ghina derived), the nasb, sanad, and rukbani.[citation needed]


Early Islamic period

Al-Kindi (801–873 AD) was a notable early theorist of Arabic music. He was joined by  al-Farabi (872–950) in proposing the addition of a fifth string to the oud. Al-Farabi published several tracts on musical theory, including the cosmological connotations of music. He identified twelve tones on the Arabic musical scale, based on the position of the fingerson the strings of the oud. Al-Farabi wrote a notable book on Islamic music titled Kitab al-Musiqa al-Kabir (The Great Book of Music). His Arabian tone system is still in use. Abulfaraj (897–967) wrote the Kitab al-Aghani, an encyclopedic collection of poems and songs that contains over 20 volumes in modern editions. Al-Ghazali (1059–1111) wrote a treatise on similar music in Persia in which he declared "Ecstasy means the state that comes from listening to music."
In 1252, Safi al-Din developed a new form of musical notation, where rhythms were indicated by geometric representation. – A similar geometric representation would not appear in the Western world until 1987, when Kjell Gustafson published a method to represent a rhythm as a two-dimensional graph.


Al-Andalus

By the 11th century, Islamic Iberia had become a center for the manufacture of musical instruments. These instruments spread gradually throughout France, influencing French troubadours, and eventually reaching other regions of Europe. The English words lute, rebec, and naker are derived from Arabic oud, rabab or Maghreb rebab, and naqareh.

grok_lead: Arabic music refers to the body of musical traditions shared among Arabic-speaking populations across the Middle East and North Africa, distinguished by its modal system of maqamat, which organize melodies through specific scales, phrases, and microtonal intervals rather than fixed Western-style keys. This system underpins improvisation and composition, often evoking tarab, an intense emotional response central to aesthetic appreciation in the tradition. Core instruments include the fretless oud lute for melodic leadership, the end-blown nay flute, the zither-like qanun, violin adapted to microtonal playing, and percussion such as the riq tambourine or darbouka goblet drum, forming the classic takht ensemble. Rhythms feature complex iqa'at patterns, typically in odd meters like 10/8 or 7/8, emphasizing polyrhythmic interplay. Emerging from pre-Islamic Arabian practices around the 5th to 7th centuries CE, where poetry recitation accompanied rudimentary percussion and lutes, Arabic music absorbed Persian, Byzantine, and indigenous elements during the Islamic expansions, leading to formalized theory by scholars like Al-Farabi in the 9th-10th centuries. The medieval Islamic Golden Age saw treatises codifying maqamat and rhythms, influencing courts from Andalusia to Baghdad, though oral transmission preserved regional variants like the muwashshah form in North Africa or tarab-oriented taqsim solos in the Levant. Modern evolutions incorporate Western harmony in urban pop and film scores by figures like Umm Kulthum, yet classical forms persist in conservatories, underscoring a continuity rooted in empirical melodic intuition over harmonic progression. While colonial and postcolonial influences introduced electrification and fusion genres, purists critique dilutions that prioritize accessibility over modal depth, highlighting ongoing tensions between tradition and globalization.
